sentences.text: Chungkingosaurus was a member of the ornithischian dinosaur group, specifically a stegosaurian, that lived in what is now China.
Even as an adult, this animal was one of the smallest stegosaurs, reaching a length of less than four meters.
Its body stood about 1.80 meters tall and it had a mass of roughly one tonne.
The main fossil specimen preserves parts of the skull, the front lower jaws, several back vertebrae, the hip bones, and the rear leg bones.
A museum model shows the creature with fourteen pairs of back plates that changed into spikes near the tail.
These defensive spikes were flattened on the sides and possessed sharp edges at both the front and back.
It is remarkable that an adult individual of this species was so small compared to other members of its family.
Researchers have noted that the unique arrangement of its tail spikes resembles a pin-cushion array.
Despite being built for walking on four legs, it could stand upright on its hind legs to reach high foliage.
Fossils of this dinosaur were first uncovered near the city of Chongqing in the year 1977.
The species was officially named Chungkingosaurus jiangbeiensis in 1983 by Dong Zhiming, Zhou Shiwu, and Zhang Yihong.
In 2014, Roman Ulansky proposed new names for a specific specimen, but later experts considered those names invalid and kept the original name.
This animal ate plants, following the herbivorous diet typical of all stegosaurs.
The tail appears to have carried at least five spikes, indicating a more complex defensive structure than usually seen.
The broader family group for this dinosaur is Stegosauridae.
It is classified within the subfamily known as Stegosauridae.
In 2008, Maidment and colleagues moved the animal into the family Huayangosauridae.
The shape of its skin armor links it to relatives like Kentrosaurus and Dacentrurus in the subfamily Kentrosaurinae.
Originally, Dong and his team placed it in the subfamily Stegosaurinae when they described it in 1983.
This creature lived during the Oxfordian stage of the Late Jurassic, about 156 million years ago.
Its habitat spanned the Bathonian to Callovian stages, ranging from 168.2 to 161.5 million years ago.
Gregory S. Paul suggested in 2010 that Chungkingosaurus might actually be the juvenile form of Tuojiangosaurus.
